translation: "Shut up," the optician said again, louder this time and walked faster.
"Selma seldom finds anything intimidating or unattractive.
He was absolutely right, but unfortunately he had revealed more than he should have to the voices.
"But she might just find love unattractive," the voices whispered, "It must have a reason," they said, "that the truth has been hidden for so long.
"Cowardice it was",the optician muttered shifting his leather bag onto the other hip because of both its banging and voices' nagging were gradually starting to hurt him.
"It was prudence," argued back those voices, "Fear is sometimes a good advisor", they stated humming a theme tune from an evening TV show.
Now the optician began walking slower.
The way to Selma's house usually took him ten minutes; suddenly it felt like spanning across an entire day's journey with very heavy luggage.
That was true.
The dog was the color of slush, a washed-out gray and shaggy like a purebred Irish Wolfhound with nothing else mixed in.
His body was still small, but his paws were as big as bear's paws and we all knew what that meant.
Selma remained standing in front of the kitchen bench.
She looked at the dog for a long time.
Then she looked at my father as though he were a gift outlet.
Farmer Häubel was firmly convinced that Death would be polite, just as Farmer Häubel himself had been all his life.
He was sure that Death wouldn't snatch life from him, but would gently take it from his hand.
He imagined Death softly knocking on the door, opening it only a crack and asking 'May I?, which of course Farmer Häubel would affirm.
"Absolutely," Farmer Häubel would respond, "please do come in," and Death would enter.
He'd stand at the foot of Farmer Haübel's bed and ask: "Is now a good time? I can return at a later date if not.

Farmer Haübel will sit up straight and say, "No, no, now works perfectly for me," he'd utter "best we don't postpone it again; who knows when you'll be able to return," and then Death will take a seat on the chair already positioned by the head of the bed.
Apologizing in advance for the coldness of its hands—which farmer Haübel knew wouldn't bother him—it'll then lay one on farmer Haübel's eyes.
The people in the village were troubled, you could see it in them, even though most tried not to show it.
This morning, just a few hours after Selma's dream, the villagers moved as if black ice had formed on all paths, not just outside but also in houses—black ice in the kitchens and living rooms.
They moved as if their own bodies had become totally alien to them, as if all their joints were inflamed and even the objects they handled could explode at any moment.
All day long they eyed their lives suspiciously—and everyone else's too whenever possible.

They repeatedly looked behind themselves to check whether someone might jump out with homicidal fury—someone who'd lost his mind and therefore had nothing of consequence left to lose—and quickly shifted focus ahead again because a mindless person might of course attack from front too.
They looked upwards preemptively for falling roof tiles or branches or heavy lampshades.
They avoided all animals because they believed that what was happening could emerge more easily from animals than humans.

The good-natured cows that were probably going to kick today—they steered clear off; dogs—even those really old ones that could hardly stand up anymore—were feared due to a chance that they may lunge at their throats today anyway.
On such days anything was possible—you wouldn't find it more far-fetched than an Okapi for example since rampant dachshunds could slash your throat open too.
Except for Selma's sister-in-law Elsbeth, the villagers were generally not superstitious.

They carelessly did everything that one shouldn't do in case of superstition: they sat calmly under wall clocks, even though superstition states that could cause death; they slept with their heads facing the door, despite this indicating in superstitious belief that they would soon be carried out feet-first through the same door.
They hung laundry between Christmas and New Year's, which as Elsbeth warned, was equivalent to suicide or aiding a murder according to superstition.
They didn't get startled when an owl cried at night, when a horse in the stable broke into heavy sweat or when a dog howled at night with its head down.
The train ride lasted fifteen minutes, there was no intermediate stop.

Since our first train ride, we always played the same game: We stood with our backs to the windows at the opposite train doors, Martin closed his eyes, I looked out of the door's window which was at Martin's back.
In first grade, I would list out loud everything I saw during the trip and Martin would try to memorize it all.

He did very well so that in second grade I didn't have to say anything anymore and Martin could recite almost everything that I saw through the misted up window of the train: "Wire factory," he said at exactly the moment we were passing by it.
"Now field.
Pasture.
The farm of crazy Hassel.
Meadow.
Forest.

Field.

Meadow.
Pasture.
Pasture.
Tire factory.
Village.
Pasture.

Forest tract.

Village.
"What else could it have been," said Selma, and that one could hardly confuse an okapi with any other animal.

"Well," I said, it might have also been a malformed cow, a misassembled giraffe, a whim of nature; after all, one cannot really see the stripes and rusty red color accurately at night when everything is very blurry.
"That's nonsense," Selma said while rubbing her forehead, "that unfortunately is nonsense, Luise.
She placed a slice of cheese on the bread, folded it over and put it in my sandwich box.
"Do you know exactly when you dreamed this?" she asked.
"Around three o'clock," replied Selma.

The image of the okapi had jolted her awake; she had sat upright in her bed and stared at her nightdress which in her dream she had been wearing on Uhlheck mountain; then she looked at the clock three o'clock.
"We probably should not take this too seriously"
Said Selma but sounded less convincing as detectives do on television who just received an anonymous letter.
"What's the matter?", I asked.
"Nothing", Selma trilled, opened the fridge, took out a pack of sliced cheese and some liverwurst and waved them both through the air.
"And what can we put on your school sandwich today?" she cooed.
"Little mouse," she added in a cloying voice, which was decidedly alarming.
"Cheese, please," I said, "what's wrong?" "Nothing", Selma cooed again, "I already told you.
She spread butter onto a slice of bread and because she was still flailing around a bit her wrist knocked the cheese off the table.
It seemed that now Selma stood still and gazed down at the packet of cheese on the floor as if it were something precious that had shattered into thousand pieces.
Selma had dreamed of an okapi three times in her life, and each time someone had subsequently died.
Therefore, we were convinced that dreaming of an okapi and death were irrefutably linked.
That is how our minds operate.
They can swiftly assuage us into believing that the most unrelated items are closely interconnected—for example, coffee pots and shoelaces, or deposit bottles and fir trees.
When I slept downstairs with Selma, she would tell me bedside stories with happy endings.
When I was younger, after the stories, I would always grasp her wrist, place my thumb on her pulse and imagine that the whole world did everything in sync with Selma's heartbeat.

I would imagine how the optician grinded lenses, Martin lifted a weight, Elsbeth trimmed her hedge, how the retailer stocked juice boxes on shelves, my mother layered pine branches together, my father stamped prescriptions; all of that done precisely to Selma's heart rhythm.
That always lulled me reliably to sleep.
But now at ten years old,Selma believed I was too old for that.
